newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ATHLETICS-LESS THAN EIGHT MINUTES WORK COULD EARN $1,000,000.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-LESS THAN EIGHT MINUTES WORK COULD EARN $1,000,000.

text.p: Less than eight minutes work on Saturday could make either Ethiopian Haile Gebrselassie or Algerian Noureddine Morceli an instant millionaire.
One million dollars, the biggest prize ever offered in athletics history, will go to the winner of a two mile reace between the two Africans provided he breaks the eight minute barrier.
Neither runner has wasted time speculating what he would do with the money.

When the race was first announced at the world indoor championships in March, both Gebrselassie and Morceli said that they were concentrating on winning first and would worry later about their new riches.
"This is what I am concentrating on for 1997," said Gebrselassie. "I am not interested in the world championships because I have already been a world champion twice."
Races over two miles were popular until the 1970s when they started to fall out of favour with runners and meeting promoters as the sport went increasingly metric.
The fortunes of the event declined so quickly that by 1993 only one international meeting staged a race over the distance.
However over the past four seasons the record books have been revised on such a regular basis that interest in the distance has revived.
Recent holders of the world best have included Morocco's Khalid Skah and Kenya's Moses Kiptanui.
In 1995 Gebrselassie lowered the world best to eight minutes 7.46 seconds last July Kenya's Daniel Komen improved that mark to the current world best of 8:03.54.

Most observers agree that if the pacemaking on Saturday is even, then the world best is almost certain to be reduced further unless the two main protagonists concentrate on each other and lose sight of the clock.
However breaking eight minutes and scooping the $1 million may still remain a tall order.
Komen set the present world best at a time last season when he was in top form.
The Kenyan would also have liked to have been part of the what is expected to be a historic race.
Much to his annoyance, he has been excluded because both of the featured athletes are sponsored by the sportswear company adidas, who have also put up the prize money.
Komen is sponsored by rival company Nike and former holder Kiptanui has also kept out of the clash because he runs in Reebok apparel.
Who is the favourite? The pundits suggest Gebrselassie because he has set previous world records at the Dutch venue and likes the track there.
He has been in outstanding form during an indoor season which included taking the 3,000m gold medal at the World Indoor Championships in a time close to the world best.
By contrast, Morceli has never run over two miles.
The Algerian has also publicly said that he is not taking the race too seriously and that it is only part of his build up to the Athens world championships in August.

Even so, Morceli has been training hard in the United States in recent months, having deliberately giving the indoor season a miss, and pride is unlike to let him give anything less than 100 per cent effort.
"We have not had many chances to race but now we will come together in the middle," Morceli said. "This race is a little bit different. I think it is exciting for the sport."
